description: A detailed machine-readable knowledge graph derived from the user-provided Wikipedia article text on overlay networks, with explicit entities, relationships, examples, architectural patterns, trade-offs, and source provenance. Model-expanded illustrations are marked separately from article-stated claims.

limitations: The input is a Wikipedia article excerpt, not a full technical standard.
The source article itself marks some statements citation-needed and includes a promotional-content/neutrality notice.
Examples and architecture patterns added beyond the article are explicitly labeled as model expansion.

data_model.id_policy: Stable namespace-prefixed IDs; relationship endpoints must refer to an entity or an architecture pattern ID.
data_model.source_policy: Source references point to the user-provided article and its bibliography records. Article claims are not treated as independently verified.

entities.name: Distributed hash table (DHT)
entities.description: A distributed system providing a lookup service similar to a hash table. Key–value mappings are maintained collectively by participating nodes, enabling lookup without requiring a single central index.

entities.name: Key–value pair
entities.description: A mapping from a unique key to a value, where the value may be an address, document, or arbitrary data.

entities.name: DHT keyspace
entities.description: The abstract set of possible keys, such as a set of 160-bit strings.

entities.name: Keyspace partitioning
entities.description: A scheme that divides responsibility for keys across participating nodes.

entities.name: Node identifier (ID)
entities.description: An identifier assigned to a DHT participant and used by the keyspace assignment/routing scheme.

entities.name: Key identifier
entities.description: A key used to identify a stored value or target within the DHT keyspace.

entities.name: DHT value
entities.description: Data associated with a key; examples include an address, document, arbitrary data, content metadata, or node contact information.

entities.name: Overlay network
entities.description: A logical network formed by links among DHT participants on top of the underlying network.

entities.name: Underlay network
entities.description: The physical/IP network that transports messages between overlay participants.

entities.name: Overlay topology
entities.description: The logical graph formed by DHT nodes and their neighbor/routing-table links.

entities.name: Neighbor node
entities.description: A node referenced by another node's routing table or neighbor set.

entities.name: DHT routing table
entities.description: A node-local set of links or neighbor information used to forward lookup messages.

entities.name: Key-based routing
entities.description: Routing messages toward the node responsible for a key using keyspace relationships.

entities.name: Greedy key-based routing
entities.description: At each step, forward a request to a neighbor whose node ID is closer to the target key; the article notes this need not be globally optimal.

entities.name: DHT lookup
entities.description: Retrieval of the value associated with a key, commonly described as get(k).

entities.name: DHT put operation
entities.description: Insertion/publication of a key–value mapping, commonly described as put(k, data).

entities.name: Membership churn
entities.description: Ongoing participant arrivals, departures, and failures.

entities.name: Autonomy and decentralization
entities.description: The nodes collectively form the DHT without a central coordinating authority.

entities.name: Fault tolerance
entities.description: The ability to remain reliable while participants join, leave, or fail.

entities.name: Scalability
entities.description: The ability to function efficiently with very large numbers of participants.

entities.name: Exact-match search
entities.description: DHTs directly support lookup by a specific key; the article contrasts this with keyword search.

entities.name: Content-addressable storage
entities.description: Using a hash of file content as a key, so lookup does not depend on the file name.

entities.name: Hash function
entities.description: A function that maps an input such as a file name, file content, or server/key pair to a hash value.

entities.name: SHA-1
entities.description: A hash algorithm used as an illustrative example in the article's 160-bit-key put/get walkthrough; the article notes real implementations may use other hash functions.

entities.name: Consistent hashing
entities.description: A key assignment technique in which nodes own nearby regions of a keyspace and membership changes affect only a limited set of keys.

entities.name: Rendezvous hashing / Highest Random Weight (HRW) hashing
entities.description: A key assignment technique in which clients hash each candidate server and key, then assign the key to the server with the highest weight.

entities.name: Locality-preserving hashing
entities.description: A family of approaches that assigns similar keys to similar objects/nodes, potentially enabling more efficient range queries.

entities.name: Keyspace distance
entities.description: An abstract distance function used to compare keys and node IDs; it is not necessarily geographic distance or network latency.

entities.name: Chord
entities.description: A DHT protocol using consistent hashing on a circular keyspace.

entities.name: Circular keyspace
entities.description: Chord's conceptual ring in which node IDs are points and a node owns a contiguous segment of keys preceding it clockwise.

entities.name: Range query
entities.description: A query for a set or interval of related keys; locality-preserving schemes can make such queries more efficient.

entities.name: Node arrival
entities.description: A participant joins the DHT and may cause limited key reassignment and routing-table maintenance.

entities.name: Node departure
entities.description: A participant leaves the DHT and may cause reassignment and routing maintenance.

entities.name: Node failure
entities.description: A participant becomes unavailable, requiring fault handling or key reassignment.

entities.name: DHT data redundancy / replication
entities.description: Storing a key–value pair on more than one suitable node to improve reliability.

entities.name: Responsible node
entities.description: The node or replica set assigned to maintain a given key or keyspace region.

entities.name: Iterative lookup
entities.description: A lookup process that discovers suitable/closer nodes before publishing or retrieving data, used by advanced DHT implementations such as Kademlia.

entities.name: Self-healing DHT behavior
entities.description: Forwarding or correcting placement when a node detects that a key belongs nearer another node, alongside presence publication and lookup.

entities.name: Node presence publication
entities.description: Publishing node IDs or contact/presence data so that lookup and routing operations can discover participants.

entities.name: Operation batching
entities.description: Combining multiple operations directed to the same node into a batch to reduce message overhead.

entities.name: Batch condensation
entities.description: Combining duplicate or reducible operations in a local batch before sending them.

entities.name: Navigable small-world network
entities.description: A topology balancing short routes against a manageable number of neighbors.

entities.name: Node degree
entities.description: The number of neighbors maintained by a node.

entities.name: Route length
entities.description: The number of hops traversed by a lookup route.

entities.name: Network diameter
entities.description: The maximum shortest-path distance between nodes in a graph.

entities.name: Big O notation
entities.description: Asymptotic notation used to describe how neighbor count and route length scale with the number of nodes.

entities.name: DHT security
entities.description: Design measures against malicious participants and attacks; decentralization alone does not guarantee security.

entities.name: Sybil attack
entities.description: An attack in which one adversary presents multiple identities/participants to influence or control a distributed system.

entities.name: Byzantine fault tolerance
entities.description: A family of mechanisms intended to tolerate malicious or arbitrary faulty behavior by participants.

entities.name: Whanau
entities.description: A DHT design described by the article as intended to resist Sybil attacks.

entities.name: Social-trust-based Sybil defense
entities.description: Using trust relationships between participants as part of a DHT design to reduce Sybil vulnerability.

entities.name: Electric routing
entities.description: An algorithmic approach referenced by the article in connection with social-trust relationships and Sybil-defense research.

entities.name: Tonika / 5ttt
entities.description: A system name associated in the article with a proposed approach using social trust and electric routing; described as research/implementation effort in the supplied text.

entities.name: Keyword search
entities.description: Search based on terms rather than a specific exact key; the article says basic DHTs do not directly provide this.

entities.name: Distributed system
entities.description: A system whose responsibilities and data are spread among multiple networked participants.

entities.name: Peer-to-peer (P2P) networking

entities.description: A search method that broadcasts a query to many or all peers, potentially avoiding a central index but creating high traffic.

entities.name: Dynamic querying

architecture_patterns.name: Basic DHT put/get lifecycle

steps.action: Choose a logical object identifier such as a filename or content identifier.
Apply the system's hash/key derivation function to obtain key k.
Send put(k, data) to any participating DHT node.
Forward the message through the overlay toward the node responsible for k.
Store the key and value at the responsible node or configured replica set.
A reader derives the same key k and sends get(k) to any DHT node.
Route get(k) through the overlay and return the stored value or a result from a replica.

architecture_patterns.grounding: Based on the supplied article's 160-bit-key put/get walkthrough. Replication step is a general implementation option described elsewhere in the article.

architecture_patterns.name: Consistent-hashing membership change

steps.action: Assign each node an identifier in the abstract keyspace.
Assign each key to the closest node according to the algorithm's keyspace distance.
When a node joins or leaves, recompute affected ownership.
Transfer only keys whose responsible ownership changed, while other key assignments remain unchanged.

architecture_patterns.grounding: Based on the supplied article's description of consistent and rendezvous hashing.

architecture_patterns.name: Kademlia-style iterative lookup and publication

steps.action: Publish or discover node-presence information in the DHT.
Start a lookup for key k and consult known routing-table neighbors.
Query closer/suitable nodes iteratively instead of flooding every participant.
Select suitable nodes for storing or retrieving the value.
Send put(k, data) to those suitable nodes; use implementation-specific repair/self-healing when placement is stale.

architecture_patterns.grounding: Based on the supplied article's description of advanced DHTs such as Kademlia.

architecture_patterns.name: DHT Sybil threat and defense concepts

steps.action: An adversary attempts to participate under many identities.
Those identities may influence routing, key ownership, or availability depending on the DHT design.
Possible defenses discussed by the article include carefully designed Byzantine fault tolerance, Whanau-style design, and social-trust approaches.
Treat defenses as design-specific; the article describes the general Sybil-defense problem as an open research question.

architecture_patterns.grounding: Based on the supplied article's security section; this is an explanatory threat model, not a claim that every DHT is vulnerable in the same way.

tradeoff_matrix.benefit: Can identify and route to destinations independently of their currently known IP address.
tradeoff_matrix.cost_or_limit: Requires overlay-level naming, lookup, or routing mechanisms.

tradeoff_matrix.benefit: Can select overlay-node sequence and apply application/site/user-specific policies.
tradeoff_matrix.cost_or_limit: Cannot directly control the underlay's route between two overlay nodes.

tradeoff_matrix.benefit: Can detect path degradation and reroute at the overlay layer.
tradeoff_matrix.cost_or_limit: Still depends on lower-layer availability and may choose a longer path.

tradeoff_matrix.benefit: Can provide logical isolation and optionally encryption.
tradeoff_matrix.cost_or_limit: An overlay by itself does not guarantee confidentiality, authentication, or secure endpoint behavior.

tradeoff_matrix.benefit: Enables logical networks and tunnels over shared infrastructure.
tradeoff_matrix.cost_or_limit: Additional headers consume capacity and can affect MTU/fragmentation behavior (MTU note is model-expanded).

tradeoff_matrix.benefit: Can prioritize traffic by application, user, or site.
tradeoff_matrix.cost_or_limit: DiffServ prioritization does not itself guarantee end-to-end throughput.

tradeoff_matrix.benefit: Can distribute data among peers without relying on router-level IP multicast.
tradeoff_matrix.cost_or_limit: Requires maintaining an overlay topology and may create redundant transmissions.
